title: ‘Anyone can enjoy art’ | Palmer Museum of Art serves students, community alike
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Palmer Museum of Art on University Park campus houses the largest collection of art between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

Palmer, located on 650 Bigler Rd., is a free-admission art museum that serves both Penn State and Central Pennsylvania alike. It offers a plethora of programs and tours, and frequently features new art exhibitions. It’s open Wednesday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Thursday’s hours are extended to 8 p.m., and Sunday's hours are from noon to 5 p.m.

Director Amanda Hellman has only been in her position at the museum for eight months, but she said she constantly strives to create a welcoming space.

“Every day feels very different,” Hellman said. “I spend a lot of time meeting with everybody, setting a vision for the institution and helping people establish workflows and how we accomplish that.”

Since assuming her position at the Palmer, Hellman has set forth big goals for the museum by creating an exhibition program for the next five years, working toward accreditation with the American Alliance of Museums and ensuring the new building is meeting the community's needs.

“This (accreditation) is important because it allows us to get bigger grants and to partner with other credited institutions, because they know that we’re following best practices,” Hellman said.

Along with that initiative, another important part of the museum's philosophy is Penn State’s land-grant mission, which is a three-fold commitment to teaching, research and public service aimed at benefiting all residents of the Commonwealth.

For Janine Yorimoto Boldt, Palmer Museum’s curator of American art, it's a vital part of her job. As a curator, Boldt thinks carefully about how to make those connections between the university, students, faculty and researchers as they study and interpret American art.

It’s important, Boldt said, to take into consideration the origins of the land-grant, as the land-grant mission relied on the sale of lands that are native lands and the dispossession of indigenous communities to fund the university.

“I have a long-term goal of a project that will think through the entangled histories of land-grant universities and indigenous dispossession through the visual arts,” Boldt said.

Recently, Boldt has purchased two photographs by native photographers Tom Jones and Ryan RedCorn, who represent contemporary native individuals. She said she wanted to grow their collection to include positive representations of native people by native artists.

On Oct. 8 at 5:30 p.m., RedCorn will deliver a speech and install his own photograph. He will also meet with the Indigenous Peoples' Student Association and the Indigenous Faculty and Staff Alliance at Penn State.

Boldt’s largest project, currently, is planning for a complete reinstallation of the American art galleries on the museum’s first floor.

“I’m spending a lot of time browsing our collection, doing research, thinking about how to reorganize and reinterpret that collection,” Boldt said.

As the museum approaches the reinstallation, Boldt said she is thinking of key themes for each of the galleries, and how they can remain flexible to allow for a regular rotation of artworks.

“(Boldt) really sought faculty, student and community member input on reimagining the American galleries, which is the strength of the museum’s collection,” Keri Mongelluzzo, the museum’s educator for academic engagement and access, said.

For students looking to get involved, the Palmer offers numerous opportunities; there’s something for everyone. Students can become ambassadors and interns, or they can merely attend events like “Art After Hours.”

Mongelluzzo oversees the undergraduate internship program at the Palmer to manage and provide leadership for the students. She said it’s open to students from all colleges to work in various museum departments.

She also organizes class visits for all colleges on campus, working with faculty to align the museum's collections to what they’re teaching. She said they teach through art to help students develop the core skills and concepts relevant to their disciplines.

Last year, Palmer had roughly 200 curricular engagements with classes. This fall, it’ll host around four to six class visits every Thursday.

Amanda Demuth, a fourth-year studying art history and philosophy, has been a student intern at the museum for three years. She’s worked with Mongelluzzo on public programming, and this year, she’s assisting Boldt with research.

“You don’t have to know anything about history, anything about art in order to intern or volunteer for the museum because there are people there that want to help you,” Demuth said.

As an undergraduate student, Demuth said her internship with the Palmer has helped her gain knowledge and perspective that she otherwise wouldn’t have experienced in a classroom setting. She said Mongelluzzo has shown her that professionalism doesn’t always have to be cut and dry.

“It’s just a good way to get involved, not just with a student community, but also with the State College community,” Demuth said.

Her favorite aspect of the museum, she said, is being able to reach communities that wouldn’t normally feel like they’re welcome in museums.

“Anyone can enjoy art, anyone can go to a museum and love it,” Demuth said. “You don’t have to understand everything.”

Anyone who’s interested in visiting the Palmer soon can look forward to the first “Art After Hours” event, which will take place Sept. 24 from 5 to 8 p.m. This event allows students to create their own art, as well as hear from Penn State student artists featured in the museum’s current exhibition titled “Dreaming American Futures: Invitational 250.”

“Come spend your time here, study here, look at stuff, challenge yourself, bring friends,” Mongelluzzo said.

title: Penn State vs. Marshall preview | Weather, injury updates and more
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Matt Campbell era is finally here.

Penn State will open the 2026 season on Saturday, facing Marshall at 3:30 p.m. in Beaver Stadium.

The Nittany Lions have won the last six straight season openers and will be looking to do so again this weekend.

Here’s a look at what to expect Week 1, from weather to betting odds and more.

Forecast

After a week of rain and thunderstorms, Saturday’s forecast will be great for the first game of 2026.

According to AccuWeather, there’ll be a high of 77 degrees, with a real feel of 80 degrees, on Saturday. As the evening rolls around, it will move to a high of 54 degrees and a real feel of 56 degrees.

There’s only a 20% chance of precipitation on Saturday, and it’s expected to be less humid than earlier in the week.

Betting, how to watch

The Nittany Lions are the heavy favorites over Marshall.

Penn State is a 24.5-point favorite over the Thundering Herd, according to FanDuel. The over/under is set at 52.5 points. These odds mean Penn State is expected to have a 38-14 victory.

The matchup will be broadcast on Fox Sports 1, while tickets are available on Ticketmaster for as low as $10.

About Marshall

The Thundering Herd are coming off a 2025 campaign where they went 5-7, including a 45-7 loss against their only Power Four opponent, Georgia.

However, Marshall returns several players this year who are slated for improved seasons, including quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson.

Del Rio-Wilson served as a dual-threat quarterback last year, throwing for 2,043 and rushing for 749 yards — both team highs. The redshirt senior has some high expectations, as he was named to the Davey O’Brien Award watch list in August, an honor given annually to the top quarterback in the country.

Outside of Del Rio-Wilson, Marshall has few other options in the run game. It has just four running backs on its roster, with only one averaging multiple carries per game last season.

Marshall’s leading receiver Demarcus Lacey and top defender Boogie Trotter have faced eligibility lawsuits throughout the offseason, but are on the official roster as of Thursday afternoon. It’s unclear whether they’ll be available on Saturday.

Returning tight end Toby Payne recorded the next-highest receiving yards last year with 393 yards and three touchdowns.

Two of the defenders Penn State will need to keep an eye on are linebacker Javae Gilmore and defensive lineman Braydin Ward. Gilmore recorded 63 tackles and 11.5 tackles for loss last season, while Ward had five tackles and four forced fumbles.

About Penn State

Penn State enters the 2026 season as one of the more uncertain teams in the country, as it has 62 new faces this season, including 24 players from Iowa State.

Among the new faces are Rocco Becht, who came to Penn State as the winningest returning quarterback in college football. Becht had a down year by his standards in 2025, but he was also dealing with a torn labrum in his left shoulder and an AC joint sprain in his right.

Now healthy, Becht is in his best form yet, according to Campbell.

Taylor Mouser said Tuesday that the Nittany Lions have many weapons on offense that could be played throughout the game.

For the running backs, that includes Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace. Each of the four are expected to share time in the backfield and bring varied experience to the running back room.

Becht will have several options in the passing game as well, including seven wide receivers Mouser named as players he has trust in: Chase Sowell, Amarion Jackson, Koby Howard, Zay Robinson, Brett Eskildsen, Keith Jones Jr. and Karon Brookins.

Penn State’s tight end room, however, boasts some of the best players on the team. Campbell said at local media day to expect multiple tight ends to be on the field at a time, with the three main guys being Benjamin Brahmer, Andrew Rappleyea and Gabe Burkle.

Defensively, several players are expected to play big roles for the Nittany Lions.

Linebacker Tony Rojas and cornerbacks Zion Tracy and Audavion Collins are among the more experienced returners on Penn State’s roster. However, transfers Kooper Ebel, Jeremiah Cooper and Marcus Neal Jr. also bring a fair share of experience to the defense.

Injury updates

Cooper, Burkle and linebacker Alex Tatsch are still recovering from long-term injuries, but all three are back practicing with the team.

Campbell said Tuesday that Cooper is the closest to returning, giving his star safety a “probable” designation for Saturday.

Burkle and Tatsch, meanwhile, are “doubtful.”

title: No.13 Penn State women’s volleyball set for Wrigley Field matchup with No. 3 Kentucky
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions arrive off of a successful Penn State Invitational performance, sweeping its opponents in two out of its three wins throughout the weekend. Up next, the blue and white will travel to play No. 3 Kentucky at Wrigley Field.

The Nittany Lions beat both Hofstra and UConn 3-0, while also escaping with a 3-2 win in a gritty battle with High Point.

After a long awaited debut, Alexis Stucky finished her first appearance in a blue and white uniform with 27 assists, six blocks, nine digs and an ace against UConn.

Stucky was not the only one making her first Happy Valley appearance. Freshman Danielle Whitmire also saw playing time, putting up five assists to aid the Nittany Lions in their sweep victory.

Graduate student outside hitter Whitney Lauenstein put up big numbers this weekend, leading the blue and white in its final two wins against High Point and Hofstra. Lauenstein totaled three digs and 14 digs against Hofstra and contributed three aces and six kills in the win against High Point.

Going into the match against Kentucky, the Stucky-Launstein duo will be dangerous. Kennedy Martin, senior right side hitter, was named MVP of the Invitational, after she added 17 kills, and three aces while hitting over .500.

Kentucky has played five games so far, only losing once to Pittsburgh with a score of 3-1. Each of their wins has been a sweep.

Heading into Sunday, Kentucky last faced UCLA, where they dominated 3-0. A large portion of their offense against the Bruins was aided by their stunning seven aces.

Notre Dame transfer Morgan Gaerte led the Wildcats in the sweep, 16 kills. Senior outside hitter Brooklyn DeLeye added onto Gaerte’s hits, pairing 15 kills of her own.

This isn’t the first time the Gaerte-DeLeye duo has come together to dominate the Wildcat offense. In Kentucky’s season opener against Wisconsin, the pair combined for a total of 22 kills to sweep the Badgers.

The Gaerte-Delaye tag team could pose a competitive front against Penn State’s Stucky-Martin duo backed by Lauenstein.

Kentucky is putting forth a very similar squad to last year, only losing one significant player, outside hitter Eva Hudson. Other than that, experience and chemistry is rooted in Kentucky’s starting line as Asia Thigpen, Georgia Watson, Hannah Benjamin and Bellamie Beus are all returning.

Because of this, SEC conference coaches favored Kentucky to win the SEC title for the tenth time this year.

On the contrary, Penn State is reshaping a partly new squad, with a balanced mix of returners and newcomers. The blue and white are welcoming seven new players, including four freshmen and three transfers; the most notable transfer being Stucky, a long-time teammate of Martin at Florida.

The seven newcomers will be joined by notable returners including Martin, Emmi Sellman, Caroline Jurevicius and Gabrielle Nichols.

In program history, the Nittany Lions have seen the Wildcats a total of eight times so far, as Penn State won seven of the meetups. While history is on Penn State's side, the most recent match, just last year, was taken by Kentucky.

The Wildcats traveled to University Park almost exactly a year ago from when they were set to play on Sunday. Kentucky won this match in a sweep. The blue and white were outplayed in kills, aces, digs, assists and blocks.

MORE VOLLEYBALL COVERAGE

title: Where to find Penn State's local music scene
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s local music scene has exploded within the last few years. Not only has the scene become a place for homegrown acts to flourish, but it's slowly becoming a staple destination for local bands and artists from other college towns wanting to expand their fanbase.

Today’s typical concert experience consists of monopolies like Ticketmaster skyrocketing their prices, sliding in obscene hidden fees at the last second, all for you to sit in bumper-to-bumper traffic on your way to pay $45 for a parking spot in the dusty, back corner of a lot.

Once you’re finally in the stadium, you’re hemorrhaging your bank account for a pretzel and a bottle of water — just to sit in the nosebleeds while your favorite band plays on the other side of the stadium.

So, what are students starting to do in lieu of not having the budget for a big name concert? They’re turning to their own local music scene.

At Penn State, the community around the streets of venues on College and Beaver Avenue are not just fans of music, but of watching their peers and their friends get on stage and give the whole crowd a night they wished they could repeat.

Manny’s

The first pit stop for anyone looking to get more invested in the local scene is Manny’s Live Performance Space. Since early 2025, this all-ages club has been a go-to venue for any band or musician looking for a fun, open space to display their talents and put on a great show.

As you descend the stairs into the main area, you’re greeted with the poised faces of music legends like Bob Dylan, Lou Reed and Frank Zappa plastered on the walls. Then, you enter the low-lit, wood-paneled room. The stage is low and the floor can get just tight enough to where you can feel the energy of the crowd, but you’re not sweating in a claustrophobic panic, allowing you to be fully immersed in the band you went to see.

According to Manny's website, it’s “ designed for those who value creativity, connection and meaningful hospitality.” The attendees of these late night, underground, musical rendezvous surely live up to that statement.

Every person in attendance at these shows is moving and grooving no matter who’s up on stage. It’s pure energy and acceptance all around.

Movin’ On

For those not looking to pay for tickets, there are many fraternities around campus that will often host local bands to play for functions during the year.

Another huge event for student acts and fans of local music is the Movin’ On BATTLE and subsequent Movin’ On Festival. At the Movin’ On BATTLE, a handful of student bands and artists are selected to compete for the opening slot of Penn State’s Movin’ On Festival.

Last year’s festival included Slayyyter and Zara Larsson — so you can catch some big names all for the humble price of $0.

Mojofest

Back in April 2026, Penn State held its first ever Mojofest Happy Valley, another huge step in cultivating a community of local and student bands. It was the first time the festival had been held at a campus outside of Massachusetts.

Mojofest is a chapter of Local Mojo, an Amherst, Massachusetts-based organization started in 2021. April’s event featured several young bands and DJs from the Penn State area.

Local Mojo has helped student bands across six different chapters find performance spaces, promotion, media and anything else that will help more people come out and watch a show.

Now, while there are several places and events for you to see live bands, let's find out just exactly who’s playing around town.

Local bands

Some of the most popular acts brought up in Happy Valley are killer bands like Sarasota, Amelia and Sequoia (last year's Movin’ On BATTLE winners), the hard-rocking trio Tuck&Roll, Ham on a Stick and 346 Sunrise. And those are just a few of the well-beloved Penn State groups that are starting to make a name for themselves both in and out of State College.

What’s so great about Penn State’s local scene is that it’s incredibly welcoming and exciting for other underground acts to come through and play alongside some of the more local groups. Bands like the popular Amherst, Massachusetts three-piece Morrissey Blvd, the Harrisburg-based Jay Veil and SKORTS all the way from Brooklyn.

By and large, Penn State’s passion and commitment to supporting local music will only grow more and more from here on out. People have a taste of what it’s like to head down to Manny’s or stop by a frat house to see a few of their friends get on stage and give them a loud night full of jams and laughs.

title: Penn State women's soccer ties Virginia Tech after late equalizer
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State had a chance to keep the ball rolling after two blowout wins in its previous matches. It was Pride Night at Jeffrey Field on a hot Thursday night as Virginia Tech came into Happy Valley. Ultimately, the Nittany Lions tied the Hokies 1-1.

1st Half

The Hokies started off the game with the ball and made good use of it. After one shot was blocked by goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress, a couple of mistakes led to an early Virginia Tech goal. The Nittany Lions were saved when VAR called the score back due to a handball.

Penn State’s offense struggled early to get past its opponents’ first third, although the Nittany Lions still dominated possession in the first 10 minutes. The Nittany Lions best chance of an early score came off a corner with forward Aubrey Kulpa soaring the shot over the net.

After a foul from Hokies midfielder Peyton May, forward Paige Kalal was awarded a penalty kick and put one in the bottom right for the first goal of the game. The Nittany Lions took the ball up the right side of the pitch often but were always excellently defended by Virginia Tech.

Virginia Tech had its best chance of a score from a corner in the 28th minute, but after a couple of high headers, Gress came down with the ball with a nice grab. Similarly in the other box, Virginia Tech goalkeeper Julianna Trujillo had a nice save shortly after on the Nittany Lions third corner kick of the game.

A second Nittany Lion goal was taken away due to an offside after a yellow card was awarded to Hokies midfielder Gabby Ciocca for unsportsmanlike conduct. Another Virginia Tech foul and Penn State free kick ultimately ended the half.

While the stat sheet might’ve made it seem like the Nittany Lions were cruising, Virginia Tech was clearly an even match.

2nd Half

As the teams switched sides for the second half, a foul happened right off the bat, showing how physical this game was. The Nittany Lions had a great chance early but couldn’t get a shot off.

The chippiness continued through the first minutes of the half, with the Hokies committing repeated fouls in the first three minutes. Virginia Tech was finding it easier to make its way deeper into Penn State’s territory in the second, taking its first real shot in a while in the 51st minute.

Ciocca again came into play with another bad foul. Also coming into play once again is Gress with a great save off a powerful kick from Hokie forward Eliana Salama. Ciocca was finally on the other side of a foul call, which led to another close miss from Virginia Tech.

Both teams were applying heavy pressure to ball carries, often with three people swarming instantly after a pass. Past the 60th minute mark, both teams were back and forth trading semi-accurate shots, as both desperately tried to add a second score to the match.

A Hokies’ corner kick in the 67th minute got punched away by Gress, followed by an amazing lower-body save right after from the keeper, as she continued to shine throughout the match. The Nittany Lions found themselves deep in their own territory a lot through the 70-minute mark, but held strong.

Penn State flipped the field and earned a corner, but the short pass turned into a shot that sailed high. The blue and white maintained possession, earning another corner, but came up empty again. The most common sound in this game was the referee's whistle, with the physicality eclipsing the entire match.

Ciocca appeared this time on the other side of a yellow card, which was given to Nittany Lions forward Ellie Kocher in the 82nd minute. Gress showed out once again with a deflection, but it was followed by another quick shot from Ciocca to tie the game 1-1 in the 84th minute.

Trujillo also continued her great play with two nice saves in the last minute of the game to keep the result a tie.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions travel to Columbus to start conference play against the Ohio State Buckeyes at 7 p.m. next Thursday.

title: Sandusky to cancel evidentiary hearing; seeks federal habeas relief
author: Kahlie Wray | Editor-in-Chief
description:
Jerry Sandusky is seeking the cancellation of his Tuesday evidentiary hearing, in which one of the men who alleged the former Penn State assistant coach assaulted him when he was young, was expected to recant his testimony.

Sandusky, 82, is instead seeking federal habeas relief — a legal procedure where individuals can challenge their detention — according to reporting from ESPN.

He was convicted in 2012 of 45 counts of child sexual abuse young boys. He was originally sentenced to 30 to 60 years in prison.

The individual who was expected to recant in the hearing, wrote in a June 2025 affidavit his original testimony "was shaped by systemic influences, not personal experiences — by investigators and prosecutors whose professional and reputational interests were tied to my cooperation."

On Friday at 1 pm, a status conference will be held to review Sandusky's request.

title: Penn State ‘forced’ to play QB Alex Manske this season after strong fall camp showing
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When recruiting Alex Manske, Matt Campbell thought of him as the “quarterback of the future” at Iowa State, he said on Aug. 7. But when the redshirt freshman had to undergo open-heart surgery as a result of a dilated aortic root and a dilated ascending aorta, that future appeared to be in jeopardy.

Manske returned to practice this fall, and he has greatly impressed Penn State’s staff. Campbell and offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser both said on Tuesday that he’d see the field this season.

“Alex has certainly deserved the right to be able to get on the field,” Campbell said. “I think even a year ago, if you watched us play, we were able to find ways to get him into the football game and impact the football game in a positive way.”

Rocco Becht, who has been a mentor to Manske throughout their shared time, shared the importance of the young quarterback seeing the field at this stage in his career. He noted that getting reps as early as possible will be key to his potential rise to the starting role.

“The more reps that (Manske) gets is going to be the best thing for him,” Becht said. “Because in the future, when all the seniors are gone and it's his team, he's going to be able to rock and roll.”

Mouser gave insight as to what Manske can do differently than other quarterbacks, noting how his ball-carrying skills and tenacity on the run give the Nittany Lions the ability to attack defenses in different ways. Additionally, Mouser has been impressed with Manske’s “gigantic,” 6-foot-3, 210-pound frame.

Because of the way Manske has played this offseason, Mouser said that he’s “forced” to play him.

Mouser shared that quarterbacks coach Jake Waters “has done a really good job” of bringing Manske up as a passer. With the first game of the season rapidly approaching, Mouser said that Manske has come a long way in the pocket.

“We can bring Alex in and be able to run unique personnel with extra alignment or not, and be able to run Alex because he's really good with the ball in his hands,” Mouser said. “I think I've seen him grow just his consistency in the passing game with how accurate he is, his ball placement, his timing, knowing where to go with the football for being a young guy.”

Manske’s story of recovery and subsequent return to action has rallied his teammates to his side. Those who were with him at Iowa State, such as Becht and Trevor Buhr, aren’t surprised by the way he’s carried himself since his return.

Campbell spoke earlier this offseason about how the entire team will fight for Becht, and Buhr said Tuesday that it’s the same case with Manske.

“Manske is a dog,” Buhr said. “Even last year, his confidence, his ability to lead the offense when we're out there. I think he's a great player and it's easy to rally behind him. We’ll always do everything we can for him, and he's going to do everything he can for us. With everything he can do, there's nothing you can't do. I'm excited to see him get his opportunity and play some ball.”

title: Penn State women's soccer hosts Virginia Tech riding in-form play
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
After defeating Bucknell on the first home opener, 5-0 Aug. 27 and Brown 6-0 on senior night Aug. 30, Penn State has a chance to continue its win streak heading into the third game on their home turf.

The Nittany Lions are set to face Virginia Tech for Pride Night at 7:30 p.m on Thursday.

The last time the two teams met on the court was during the 2014 NCAA Round of 16, when the blue and white defeated the Hokies 2-1 at Jeffrey Field. This was the only time in program history the two competed, potentially giving Virginia Tech the fire under their boots to tie up the playing field this week.

What to watch for Virginia Tech

The Hokies are looking to continue their win streak after defeating Georgetown 2-1 and William & Mary 3-1 this past week. Virginia Tech is yet to tally a loss, sitting at 4-0-2 at the beginning of their season, which makes for an impressive 0.833 winning percentage.

The maroon and orange captain Anna Weir accounted for all three goals during the Hokies' road win against William & Mary, making her the 13th Hokie to record a hat trick in program history. The senior forward is Virginia Tech’s leading scorer and point holder, as she stands as someone to watch out for in Thursday’s matchup.

Forward graduate student Eliana Salama is another notable player to watch in the attacking third as she has marked 42 shots with two goals and four assists.

On the offensive, the Hokies are averaging 21 shots and 2.83 goals. Their gameplay this season suggests Virginia Tech dominates possession and successfully creates chances for points, meaning the blue and white will have to employ a tight-knit back line.

What to watch for Penn State

Penn State is coming into Thursday hot after two milestone performances. Coach Erica Damback secured her 300th career win following the Bucknell match and redshirt freshman Nikki Crane posted the program’s 26th hat trick in her phenomenal performance against Brown.

There isn’t a doubt the Nittany Lions suffered major offensive losses from last season, but junior forward Aubrey Kulpa and Crane have both shown to fill the gaps as attacking forces. The two are leading the team in points and has an efficient mark on shots-on-goal percentage, with Kulpa at 0.727 and Crane at 0.750.

With Virginia Tech being a team that dominates possession, the blue and white are going to have to be connected on the defensive end. Defenders Kayleigh Herr and Bella Ayscue will need to continue their communication to hold together the back line and potentially add another clean sweep to Penn State’s score sheet.

With the last and only matchup between the teams being rewarded to the Nittany Lions in their own backyard, the blue and white have the upper hand this Thursday as Virginia Tech is once again the traveling team.

Both teams are walking onto the pitch at Jeffrey Field with one opportunity, fighting to protect their win streak.

title: Penn State field hockey heads into another busy home weekend
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State enters the upcoming weekend of competition after its first win of the season over Lock Haven 8-0, with a current 1-1 record after dropping its season opener to No. 5 Virginia 4-3 in a close overtime match.

The blue and white will have a chance to build up its win column, as both opponents this weekend are coming in unranked.

Villanova

Villanova arrives to this matchup 2-0 after a 2-1 win over Delaware, followed by a shutout victory against La Salle. Penn State and the Wildcats are both coming off of huge shutouts of seven or more goals, indicating both teams have powerful offenses.

The blue and white’s leading offensive players are Joji Purdy, Sienna Dunn and Chloe D’Hage. All three have contributed one or two goals so far and hold a total of five points. Apart from Purdy and D’Hage, who are both underclassmen, Dunn is a first-year international graduate student.

On Villanova’s side, the top offensive player to look out for is Gemma Lysaght. The senior has put up four goals for her team and amassed 11 points already in the two games this season. Just behind Lysaght is Ava Borkowski, who has scored two goals for the Wildcats so far.

In goal is senior Maddi Sears, who played all of the time in net for the Wildcats. The Avondale, Pennsylvania, native only allowed one goal over the two contests, yet faced heavy action with 15 total saves to amass an impressive 0.938 save percentage.

The two big cats will meet Friday at 3 p.m.

Delaware

Following Friday’s matchup, Penn State takes on Delaware at noon on Sunday. This will be the second weekend in a row where the Nittany Lions have a quick turnaround to perform in another home game.

Delaware started its season with a close loss to Villanova 2-1, but was able to overcome No. 18 Monmouth last Sunday with the same score going the Blue Hens' way. With these close matches, Delaware is keeping up its defensive end by only allowing three goals so far this season.

On the offensive side of the ball, the Blue Hens don’t have any clear offensive piece, with three clear goals spread across three players: Penelope Kousouris, Alexa Michielsen and Livia Van't Hek. For Delaware, only Lexi Causa has logged an assist so far this season, as two of the three scores came unassisted.

Delaware has debuted two goalkeepers this season: Jane Baldy and Gabby Prentice. Baldy played for the second half of the Villanova game, allowing one goal and having one save. Prentice started the Villanova game, allowing one goal with no saves. Prentice started the second game and played all 60 minutes, helping her team secure the win by allowing one goal and making one save. Leading the Blue Hens is coach Tara Zollinger, a three-time DII National Champion in her second season after leading Delaware to a conference championship in her first season.

On the Penn State side, Aby Deverka returns for her third season and is the sole goalkeeper for the Nittany Lions. Starting and playing in each game, she has allowed four goals this season but collected six saves.

As Penn State heads into the weekend, it’s building up that strong momentum on both sides of the ball with its coach, Hannah Prince, in her opening season.

title: Inside Agostino Abbatiello, Paul Robinson preliminary hearings
author: Kahlie Wray & Mia Debelevich & Grace Levy | The Daily Collegian
description:
Agostino Abbatiello, who’s been dubbed “one of the biggest drug dealers at Penn State,” was escorted into the Centre County Courthouse by law enforcement around 8 a.m. on Wednesday.

The 24-year-old from Westbury, New York, is one of the alleged ring-leaders of a fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring, according to authorities. Over the course of six hours, several individuals prosecutors say are implicated in the ring gave testimony.

Many affirmed that Abbatiello was the main supplier of cocaine at Penn State during his time as a student.

Following Abbatiello’s preliminary hearing, Paul Robinson, the father of Thomas Robinson — the other alleged ring-leader — began his.

Senior Deputy Attorney General Megan McGoron was the lead prosecutor. Centre County Common Pleas Judge Jonathan Grine presided over the court proceedings.

“On Wednesday, witnesses testified that Abbatiello boasted about his wealth and status atop the trafficking ring,” Attorney General Dave Sunday said in a press release following the hearings.

Here’s what you need to know about Wednesday’s preliminary hearings.

Agostino Abbatiello

Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, is facing 11 felonies and is being represented by Philip Masorti.

Prior to the hearing, Masorti filed a motion claiming Abbatiello was “being unlawfully held at the Centre County Correctional Facility in direct violation of his constitutional rights.”

During the bail hearing Masorti requested $200,000 unsecured bail for Abbatiello, stating he was not a danger to the public nor a flight risk. McGoron argued he was a danger to the community, as the prosecution has evidence that Abbatiello previously sent threatening messages to an individual.

Grine granted Abbatiello $250,000 secured bail. His bail conditions include no contact with witnesses, no consumption of alcohol or drugs and he must surrender his passport.

Abbatiello was released from the Centre County Correctional Jail after he posted bail Wednesday afternoon.

Thomas, Mohammed Huraibi, Lars Zeepvat and Detective Donald Paul all testified during Abbatiello’s preliminary hearing.

Each affirmed in their testimonies that Abbatiello was one of the main suppliers of cocaine at Penn State.

Thomas, 23, of Pittsburgh, was the first to testify. He alleged that he began discussing plans to sell cocaine at Penn State in summer 2023 with Huraibi, a Delta Upsilon brother.

Thomas bought larger portions of cocaine over time, he said. He testified that his first purchase, alongside Huraibi, was for 100 grams of cocaine. The amount Thomas purchased went up to 1,000 grams for $22,000, Thomas said.

The prosecution asked Thomas if the amount of cocaine he purchased was based on the demand from Penn State students, to which Thomas responded, “Yes.”

The two made their first purchase from Abbatiello in August 2023. Thomas testified that Huraibi would go pick up the cocaine from Abbatiello, but he did not meet Abbatiello until after Huraibi said he no longer wanted to be a part of their arrangement.

Huraibi made a group chat between the three of them to introduce Thomas to Abbatiello, he said.

Lars Zeepvat, 24, of Medham, New Jersey, also testified against Abbatiello at his preliminary hearing.

Zeepvat allegedly met Abbatiello through Robert Zanolla, another member of the Sigma Chi fraternity. The three, along with another brother who would drive, would purchase “personal amounts” of cocaine from Philadelphia, Zeepvat testified.

Abbatiello gave Zeepvat $1,500 to help him pay for Sigma Chi’s spring break trip. When Zeepvat was unable to pay him back, he “would have to sell bags for Auggie,” Zeepvat said.

By senior year, Abbatiello had become more quiet, according to Zeepvat. He said Abbatiello was spending money on various things, including a new wardrobe and a $5,000 bong; he added that Abbatiello was no longer selling to get high.

“He started selling for money, and he started selling for popularity,” Zeepvat said.

Zeepvat also alleged that Abbatiello was gambling up to $10,000. He said the two went to a bar together in July 2025, where Abbatiello informed Zeepvat he received a letter to speak in front of a grand jury. According to Zeepvat, Abbatiello told Zeepvat he would also be receiving a letter, and said, “Please don’t say anything.”

Paul Robinson

Paul, 56, of Pittsburgh, was represented by Michael DeRiso and Stephie-Anna Ramaley.

His counsel sought to have his three charges, which include hindering apprehension or prosecution by concealing or destroying evidence, dropped.

McGoron called Ryan Matson, a former Penn State student who graduated in 2025, as the prosecution’s first witness. Matson was a Delta Upsilon brother and one of Thomas’ close friends, according to his testimony.

Following Thomas’ December 2024 arrest, Matson alleged he received a phone call from Paul. When Matson picked up, Thomas answered the phone inquiring about a “package.”

According to Matson’s testimony, he was referring to a safe Thomas kept in Matson’s apartment. Matson said he did not have the key nor combination. Though he didn’t have access to the safe, he said he believed drugs were inside, based on prior interactions with Thomas.

Matson said he then told Thomas he hid the safe in the woods. He claimed to have a later conversation with Paul about retrieving the safe, which he alleges they did days after. Matson testified that Paul told him “to keep it quiet and not to tell anyone about what we had done.”

During cross-examination, DeRiso tried to establish through questioning that Matson was not sure what the contents of the safe were. Grine ultimately allowed the charges against Paul to move forward.

“Mr Robinson didn’t do anything wrong. He went to get his son’s things out,” DeRiso said to media outside of the courthouse. “Was it maybe not a smart decision to get that safe not knowing what was in it? I don’t know. But there is no evidence of what was in the safe. So again, we’re all speculating here that there’s this massive amount of cocaine in the safe with all this money.”

Remaining defendants

Thomas, Huraibi and Zanolla were scheduled to have preliminary hearings on Wednesday, but all three waived their hearings following Paul and Abbatiello’s hearings, according to a press release from Attorney General Dave Sunday.

Zeepvat was the only defendant to waive his preliminary hearing ahead of Wednesday’s testimony.

Per court documents, Zeepvat’s formal arraignment is scheduled for Sept. 9 at 1:00 p.m. with Judge Julia R. Rater. Arraignments for Robinson, Huraibi and Zanolla are scheduled for Sept. 30 at 1:00 p.m. with Judge Grine.

At the formal arraignment, each defendant will hear the charges brought against them. They will have the opportunity to submit a plea.

The eight remaining defendants in the case were charged with misdemeanors. Liam Smith, Michael Brogno, Kaden Howe, Connor Hurleigh, Seth Beardsley, Kyle Ridpath, Daniel Price and Charlie Weisman all have preliminary hearings scheduled for Oct. 14 at 8:30 a.m. with Judge Kelley Gillette-Walker.

title: Penn State men’s soccer hosts Yale Friday in final conference tune-up
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
After falling back-to-back against Missouri State and Pittsburgh, Penn State has a chance to turn the tide this week and get back in the winning column.

The Nittany Lions continue their play on Jeffrey Field against Yale at 7 p.m. Friday.

This matchup marks the third head-to-head meeting between the two programs, after both wins went the Nittany Lions way previously. Both the blue and white and the Bulldogs have an opportunity to set the tone for their new rivalry.

What to watch for Yale

Yale currently sits even heading into this game at 1-1 after suffering a loss in its opener against Quinnipiac and then bouncing back to win at Army on Aug. 31.

Over the two games, the Bulldogs have netted 5 goals on a 0.65 shots-on-goal percentage, with the scoring spread evenly across five players. Freshman Ethan Otterberg leads Yale’s points with three.

This score sheet spread suggests the Bulldogs aren’t relying on a single threat, but on multiple offensive outlets that can tally a point, reflecting similar attacking trends from their previous season, which also had no main offensive weapon.

Yale finished its conference play at 2-4-1 in 2025, leading it to be picked seventh in the Ivy League Preseason Poll.

The Bulldogs lost 10 players from their 2025 senior class, including starting goalkeeper Conrad Lee and former team captain Diego Zaffanella, but Sven Meacham is highlighted as a player to watch in this matchup.

The junior defender is coming off of a phenomenal sophomore year, tallying one goal and six assists, the most by a Yale player since Quanah Brayboy in the 2023 season and overall finishing second in the Ivy League. Meacham was named to the All-Ivy Second Team after appearing and starting in all 15 regular season games.

What to watch for Penn State

The Nittany Lions enter Friday’s contest still finding their footing, as it’s their first year under coach Rob Dow. The new boss owned the nation's ninth-best win percentage entering this season, with a chance to continue that through his years with the blue and white.

Only three players from the 2025 season returned to play under Dow this campaign. With Frederick Grundin, Joe Sheridan and Morgan Marshall being the only remaining players from that squad, there is a tall task at hand to get Penn State to gel as a cohesive unit.

Joining the roster this year is senior Amadou Kone, who has already made an identity for himself as Penn State’s current point leader at five via two goals and one assist.

Beyond the three returners, Dow brought in 6-foot-7 freshman goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese. While Grundin is the experienced returning keeper, Peluffo-Wiese has played and started in all three of the Nittany Lions matches with six saves on a 0.462 save-percentage.

Alongside Peluffo-Wiese, 6-foot-4 Noah Förster and 6-foot-6 Sheridan are paired at center back, two potential threats during set pieces and aerial duels against Yale’s offensive outlets.

Penn State gets a look at rebuilding its harmony under Dow during Friday’s matchup before its season's gameplay starts ramping up against top-caliber Big Ten programs.

title: Position preview | Penn State QBs bring experience, young talent to revitalized room
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has a completely new quarterback room for the 2026 season.

Matt Campbell needed to start from scratch when he took over in December, as Drew Allar is in the NFL with the Pittsburgh Steelers, Ethan Grunkemeyer is starting at Virginia Tech and Jaxon Smolik is still competing for the starting job at Temple.

Campbell brought his top two quarterbacks with him from Iowa State and added other pieces to round out a very versatile and unique room in his first year.

Starting quarterback

Rocco Becht will be the starting quarterback for the Nittany Lions on Saturday. That’s been assumed pretty much since he committed to Penn State out of the transfer portal.

Becht dealt with injuries to his shoulders last year, but still passed for 2,584 yards and 16 touchdowns. He eclipsed the 3,000 passing mark in the two seasons beforehand.

What makes Becht a compelling starter is his veteran presence and leadership. Becht will be the most experienced quarterback in the nation this year, and that should play major benefits to the success this season on offense.

Becht’s leadership has been highly talked about this offseason and has been key to bringing the team fully together.

Young, veteran backups

Alex Manske has reemerged as the backup ahead of Connor Barry after missing spring practice with a heart condition that required open heart surgery.

Manske is likely the future of the position, but he’s already put himself in a spot to get meaningful time in 2026, as offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser has recognized his talent.

“Alex Manske is one of the most talented guys on the offense,” Mouser said Tuesday. “We're not going to keep him off the field this year, so he's forced us to have to play him, and he's been really good, especially with going through what he did.”

The former 4-star recruit played in three games during his freshman season at Iowa State. His emergence at practice this fall has earned him a chance to play this season, as Campbell said they discuss each week how he can be involved in the game plan.

The other potential backup is Barry, who was in the backup spot this spring when Manske was sidelined. He even got some first-team reps while Becht recovered from his shoulder injuries.

Barry made his way from Christopher Newport, where he threw for 2,866 yards last year, becoming a semifinalist for the Gagliardi Trophy, the equivalent of the Heisman Trophy at the Division III level.

While Barry has no experience at the FBS level, let alone the Power Four level, his experience could come into play if he takes snaps this season. Barry’s entering his fifth year after beginning at Appalachian State in 2022 and will end his collegiate career on the Nittany Lions.

Depth behind the backups

The depth behind the first three quarterbacks has taken a hit with freshman Peyton Falzone making the move to tight end. That leaves just one true freshman at quarterback and the lone returning member of the room from 2025.

Kase Evans joined Penn State after signing with Iowa State on Dec. 3, following Campbell to Happy Valley. Evans was a 3-star recruit and the No. 67 quarterback in the 2026 class, per 247Sports composite. Evans proved he can air it out, while also having a track and field background in high school, logging a 11.69 second 100-meter dash.

Jack Lambert returned to Penn State as the lone walk-on in the room. Lambert joined the Nittany Lions in 2023 and was named the coaching staff’s Developmental Squad Offensive Player of the Week twice in his redshirt year.

title: For those new to campus, here’s what to know about UPUA
author: Jackson Malenke | The Daily Collegian
description:
As freshmen begin their search for organizations to join, the University Park Undergraduate Association (UPUA) is an option for students interested in government and policy.

Formed in 2006, the University Park Undergraduate Association (UPUA) is the official student government at Penn State. UPUA serves as the voice of the student body, as it brings student concerns to university leaders, according to its website.

As the fall semester kicks off, here is what to know about UPUA.

The branches

UPUA is split into three branches: the executive branch, the legislative branch and the judicial branch.

The executive branch, led by President Kat Hogan and Vice President Maria Lopez, carries out the day-to-day operations and administrative work.

The legislative branch, led by the speaker Ayden Meise and vice speaker James Dugery, consists of the general assembly. They write, review and vote on legislation. According to its site, they hold the only right to amend the constitution.

The judicial branch, led by Chief Justice Jude York, is run by justices who decide on internal disputes and interpret documents.

The committees

There are five core committees within UPUA. Committees advocate for student rights, write legislation and research issues within the organization.

The academic affairs committee concentrates on student academic rights and academic policy. According to the UPUA website, the committee works to change university senate policies, advocate for lower costs of educational resources and educate students about their rights.

The campus operations committee works on issues related to campus infrastructure and daily student life. The committee provides students with helpful services that impact the way they experience campus transportation, on-campus services and online services like Canvas, per its site.

The government and community committee relations manages advocacy at the local, state and federal levels. The committee takes on shared initiatives with the Borough of State College.

The justice and equity committee works to fight injustice and help marginalized students within the university and student government. The committee aims to advocate for all identities on campus, with focuses on bias and discrimination, international students’ rights, disability services and uplifting cultural celebrations, according to the site.

The student engagement and wellness committee focuses on student well-being and campus safety for all. The site says the committee works on initiatives on student safety, event planning, off-campus living, athletics, student conduct, counseling services, student health, recreational services and sexual violence awareness and prevention.

Getting involved

Freshmen can get involved with UPUA by joining the First-Year Council, an entry-level mentorship program designed for first-year students to become accustomed to the organization. The program pairs freshmen with representatives to learn from and work on projects with.

Applications are open now and close Sept. 10 at midnight.

There are also various open positions across all three branches, with most applications closing on Sept. 4. These positions include executive director of records, archivist, programming directors, deputy chief of staff, department of sustainability directors, shadowing and informational program, at-large representative, associate justice and judicial clerk. The justice and clerk’s applications are rolling.

The executive director of records oversees the UPUA’s documentation, compiles histories and uploads voting records to their website.

The archivist serves as the primary contact for members interested in researching the history of past assemblies and manages the legislation portion of the organization’s google drive by uploading legislation passed each week.

The programming directors assist with the logistical and operational aspects of the student government’s various projects and initiatives.

The deputy chief of staff oversees daily operations, coordinates projects and keeps initiatives on track.

The shadowing and informational program is a mentorship program for students looking to join UPUA. Members in the program will have the chance to watch the work representatives, committees and other departments within the organization.

The associate justice reviews cases, interprets documents and ensures everything done within the organization aligns with the UPUA Constitution.

The judicial clerk helps write briefs and deliberations on governing documents.

What to expect

General assembly meetings happen every Wednesday at 7 p.m. and are open to the general student body. In these meetings, members vote on legislation, listen to updates and coordinate campus collaborations. It sometimes opens the floor, allowing for presentations from various student groups.

At the beginning of the year, the annual budget is presented to the general assembly for a vote. Once the budget is passed, individual committees and events can begin spending.

The Steering Committee, a leadership and administrative body, meets weekly to discuss organizational direction, interview new members, review legislation and provide updates across all branches. The minutes for these meetings are open to the public.

UPUA hosts various events, such as monthly meet and greets, throughout the semester. The government also collaborates with other student groups on campus. For example, they previously collaborated with the Latino Caucus for the Latine Heritage Month Fun Friday event. Other events can be found on their Instagram or website.

title: Staff predictions | Will Penn State defeat Marshall to begin the Matt Campbell era?
author: The Daily Collegian Football Staff
description:
Beaver Stadium awaits Matt Campbell and Penn State this Saturday as fans anticipate the first game of his tenure.

Marshall will be the first test for the Nittany Lions this season, a squad they haven’t faced since 1930. The matchup kicks off at 3:30 p.m. on Fox Sports 1.

Taylor Mouser acknowledged there will be some “anxiousness” throughout the team, but it’s unclear how much of an impact that will have on Penn State.

Here’s how we think the Nittany Lions will fare in Week 1.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 34, Marshall 13

While the offseason has resulted in lots of optimism about Penn State as a whole, the team itself is still truly an unknown when it steps on the field on Saturday.

A slow start is very likely, especially with a high percentage of the team playing in Beaver Stadium in front of a full crowd for the first time. The Stripe Out will be behind Penn State, but the players will have to adjust to the buzz of the stands throughout the game.

After the adrenaline from the team entrance and the beginning of the first game wears off, the offense will start to put things together with Rocco Becht feeding a plethora of receivers against a defense that shouldn’t be able to stop the Nittany Lions on a consistent basis.

Becht will play more of the game than most people will think for multiple reasons. The quarterback hasn’t played a game since recovering from injuries to both shoulders, but the matchup will also be close throughout the first half and into the third quarter.

The defense will have to maintain Marshall quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson, who’s dual threat ability could cause issues to a defense that hasn’t played together in a game environment. However, the athletic talent of the linebackers, including Tony Rojas, will withstand Del Rio-Wilson’s legs and keep Marshall off the board consistently.

The Nittany Lions will run away with the game as it moves along, with all four of the expected running backs getting even playing time while the receivers rotate through a large group. The freshness that Penn State can bring with consistent rotations will ultimately be too much for a Marshall team that’s entering a hostile environment.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 35, Marshall 14

It’s the debut of a new era for Penn State, and I believe that the Nittany Lions will find some success on offense, leaning heavily on the skill players who transferred from Iowa State in the first half. Specifically, Becht’s connection with tight end Benjamin Brahmer will be extremely important to ease Penn State into the passing game.

Additionally, it’s a Stripe Out, and if there’s anything that I know about themed games, it makes fans go nuts. That kind of noise against an inexperienced Sun Belt team, while it won’t nearly come close to a White Out, is extremely difficult to contend with.

With that said, it’ll be interesting to see how Mouser and D’Anton Lynn play around with having different players and different angles of attack. Having a multitude of running backs and wide receivers see the field is a great way of seeing who’s better in a real game, but it’s also risky to not always utilize the experienced players.

Penn State’s defense features a lot of players coming back from injury, or playing football for the first time in at least a year. Rojas, Max Granville and potentially Jeremiah Cooper are a few names to watch as they ease back in from injury.

The nonconference schedule overall will be a test run, so it wouldn’t surprise me if Marshall charges down the field for a couple of touchdowns before the Nittany Lions settle in on defense.

All things considered, the game will be far closer than many imagine, but I think that Penn State will ultimately emerge victorious, primarily from the first half before the coaching staff starts experimenting.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 31, Marshall 10

Penn State’s roster features players from all over the country that have come together in Happy Valley for Campbell’s first season.

With that comes growing pains. It’s going to take some time for the players to mesh, so don’t expect the Nittany Lions to look perfect on Saturday. That’s why I think this game will be a bit closer than many may think.

Becht is going to be the star of the matchup for Penn State in his debut and return from shoulder injuries, but backup Alex Manske will also shine in the garbage time drives he receives, giving fans some excitement about the future.

On defense, Rojas will impress coming off his torn ACL and steal the show with his speed and agility as he did to begin 2025. The defensive line, however, will struggle to garner much pressure, with the defensive backfield stepping up to keep Marshall at bay.

The Nittany Lions will still handily win this contest, but both sides of the ball will surely have a few bumps in the road on the way to victory.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 48, Marshall 10

Campbell’s first game day is finally here. While many anticipate some opening day jitters for the Nittany Lions, I don’t think that’ll be the case.

Penn State will fight back and forth with Marshall through the opening drives, allowing 10 points to the Thundering Herd in the first half. The second half will be another story, as the Nittany Lions will issue a shutout while scoring multiple touchdowns over the final 30 minutes.

Becht will start his final year off on a strong note, throwing a pair of touchdowns. His counterpart, Manske, will have nearly a full quarter on the field, recording a combined 100 yards between his passing game and running attack.

Penn State’s three-headed running back room will all have successful days, each recording numerous carries with two of the three finding the end zone.

In addition, the three starting receivers will each record multiple receptions. Chase Sowell will lead the way, while Koby Howard will earn his first career touchdown.

Defensively, the Nittany Lions will have a hay day with Marshall. Starting quarterback Del Rio-Wilson will throw two interceptions, with Zion Tracy and Audavion Collins putting clamps on the opposing receivers.

Campbell’s first game will come effortlessly as the Nittany Lions cruise to victory in Week 1.

title: ‘He wants to be great’ | Meet Penn State HC Matt Campbell through the eyes of his former, current players
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The room goes silent halfway through Iowa State’s team meeting. All the players can hear is a faint ringing coming from someone’s seat, and now they’re all dreading the next words that’ll come out of their first-year head coach’s mouth.

“Is that a phone?” Matt Campbell asked.

Campbell had a strict no-phone policy for team meetings. Bring one in and it goes off, you’re facing the consequences. So once the culprit was found, Campbell sent everyone to the indoor field to run sideline-to-sideline sprints before practice.

In between the half-gassers, Campbell lectured the players about discipline until he finally put them out of their misery and called everyone in. He began speaking about preparation for another day of practice, but the end of his speech was not at all what any of the players anticipated.

There would be no football — they were going to a pool in the middle of fall camp instead.

“It was all planned out,” former Iowa State wide receiver Trever Ryen told The Daily Collegian. “They told the kid to have his phone go off. I think our (director of football operations) actually called the phone so it would go off in the team meeting.”

A decade later, Campbell is Penn State’s head coach after 10 unprecedented seasons at Iowa State, where he ended his stint as the winningest coach in program history. The now 46-year-old joined the Cyclones in 2016 as one of the youngest head coaches in college football — which means skipping a day of fall camp for the pool was a risky move for a somewhat unproven head coach at the time.

But Campbell has never been one to care about outside pressure or expectations. He believes if you show up every day and stay consistent in your work, good things will happen.

“I feel like his mindset of just being process-oriented and going about it day by day, and not worrying about the end result, because if you go day by day like that, the end result will come,” Ryen said. “I feel like that's what he kind of instilled in everything. But I feel like that's why he's so relentless, because he wants to be great, and he's going to be great, and he's already shown that he can be great.”

Rocketing up the ranks

When quarterback Phillip Ely decided to leave Alabama in 2013, he was hesitant about whether transferring to Toledo was the right decision for him. The Rockets’ head coach at the time seemed like the right fit, but he was slowly getting more national attention — he was the “hot, young, newer coach,” as Ely put it.

Ely worried that he’d be transferring to a program with a head coach that has one foot out the door. Campbell assured Ely that wasn’t the case.

“My conversations with him were always very genuine and honest, and he made the promise that he was going to stay there,” Ely told The Daily Collegian. “He had no plans to leave, and I trusted him.”

Even though Campbell made that promise, it was clear he was on the path to coaching stardom. He became the youngest FBS head coach when he took over Toledo at 32 years old in 2011 and had the Rockets in the top-25 for the first time in more than a decade.

Campbell’s youth only made him that much more attractive as a coach, in large part because he could relate to his players in a way others couldn’t.

“He had experience playing that wasn't too long ago,” Ely said. “I feel like he really related to us as players, and just had a real energy and spirit to him that was contagious. It definitely kind of rippled to his assistants, and they all shared and matched his energy and his passion.”

Campbell wanted players with that same passion, too. Ely said Campbell was always adamant his team was “climbing a mountain,” and he only sought guys that were “climbers.”

“He didn't want guys that were standing still,” Ely said. “He wanted guys who were constantly just chasing greatness and choosing greatness in whatever they do.”

But Campbell was climbing a mountain of his own, and by his fourth full season at Toledo 2015, it became nonsensical for him not to take another step up.

Building Ames from the ground up

After three straight seasons with three or fewer wins, Iowa State needed to make a change. So head coach Paul Rhoads was out after seven years. Campbell was in.

Running back Mitchell Harger, who had been at Iowa State since 2012, was unsure about his future after Rhoads’ departure. All four years of his career had been under Rhoads, and he was hesitant and anxious about what was next for the Cyclones.

But as he heard more and more about Campbell, that hesitation turned into excitement. He knew he had to stay or he’d be missing out on “something special.”

Once he saw Campbell start building his culture from the ground up, Harger knew he made the right decision.

“People get intoxicated with what Campbell brings to the table and what he builds around him, as far as the culture,” Harger told The Daily Collegian. “That's why you see so many people at Iowa State, who maybe could have taken better NIL offers at other places, but stuck around because of what he brings to the table.”

As the years began to pass by, Campbell’s beliefs and culture had a hold on the Cyclones, and he was still looking for players with the exact same values as he was when he first arrived.

In 2018, defensive back Greg Eisworth II was ready to move from community college to Division I football. Campbell’s selling pitch to Eisworth was the same he gave players when he took over two years prior: “I want good people. I want good leaders, because you'll turn a program around from the inside out.”

“Obviously I want to be successful and turn the program around,” Eisworth said. “But first and foremost, it was people that loved each other and cared about each other. And for me, it was like, ‘Man, I would love to be a part of this.’ Because win, lose or draw, whatever the outcome is, it felt like a family.”

Campbell’s way undeniably worked. Even as money and the transfer portal began taking over college football, he was putting one of the worst programs of all time in contention for the Big 12 each year despite limited resources.

He had chances to leave. His name was thrown around for every open job, even ones in the NFL. But Campbell stayed true to what he was building at Iowa State.

“In a world that is kind of win by any means or get it by any means, he refused to be that person,” Eisworth said. “To be a part of that, to see it, kind of affirmed who I wanted to be. It affirmed that things can be done the right way.”

‘Everybody was shocked’

Iowa State quarterback Rocco Becht heard the mumblings but brushed them off. Campbell to Penn State? It simply had to be a publicity stunt.

But for the first time, the rumors were true. Campbell stood in front of his team the night of Dec. 5 and told them he was taking the job. After 10 years of staying loyal to the Cyclones, he was finally moving on.

“I think that just goes to the fact how great of a guy he is, how much he cares about a program that he's at,” Becht said on Feb. 4. “So when he took the job, yeah, everybody was shocked, but we all knew the reasons why he took it, and so we weren't mad at him at all.”

In the ensuing days, 55 Iowa State players entered the transfer portal, with 24 following Campbell to the Nittany Lions. For many, the decision to join him was a no-brainer.

“He builds you to be a great player, but he also builds you to be a great young man,” safety Jeremiah Cooper said on Feb. 4. “Even my parents said it: ‘You got to follow him, he set you in so many ways in the future.’ Just personally, he literally changed me. I can't ask for anything more in a coach.”

Campbell’s impact at Penn State has already been felt in just eight months. He’s had the Nittany Lions consistently helping the community, and the Lasch Building walls are now covered in his ideology.

Whether on-field success that Penn State fans have been yearning for follows suit is unclear for now, but at the very least, Campbell’s culture isn’t going anywhere.

“I'm so happy that the Penn State football players get to experience what I got to experience, knowing that he's building that program based on his great values of family, trust, hard work,” Ryen said. “It's going to be awesome when those players get to come back five or 10 years down the road, or right after you graduate, and you can walk into that football building with coach Campbell and feel like it's like your house.”

title: Data center development is booming.  Here’s how it's being opposed, regulated in Pennsylvania
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
The increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) has already been the subject of several developments at Penn State. The rollout of AI Studio, which grants students, faculty and staff free access to paid models of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, is part of a university-wide push for initiatives.

The nationwide demand for increased AI capabilities has resulted in a data center construction that’s both championed and opposed across the United States and around the world.

The past, present and potential future of data centers

The concept behind data centers is not a recent one. The first data center was constructed in 1945 to house the functions of ENIAC, the world’s first programmable general-purpose electronic digital computer. The modern interpretation of data centers has already been built and used for decades to store the servers, software and networking equipment necessary to power the internet, and eventually cloud computing.

The primary format adopted to fulfill the needs of artificial intelligence is known as the hyperscale model: Campuses with multiple buildings containing the equipment needed for AI to store and process data.

Hyperscale data centers also come with additional systems meant to ensure that technology functions properly, such as cooling systems to prevent overheating, and emergency backup generators in case the data center is unable to receive power from an external grid.

According to Data Center Map, there are a total of 4,767 data centers either in operation or under development throughout the United States since they began tracking development in 2007. 174 of them are located in Pennsylvania.

A Feb. 19 analysis of DCM’s data by the Pew Research Center found that 67% of all planned data centers are located in rural areas, with 75% of this figure in the southern and midwestern United States.

John Zangari, secretary of No Data Centers in Mifflin County, said rural areas are prime locations, as they have large swathes of relatively flat and undeveloped land. A data center proposal by PA Data Center Partners and PowerHouse Data Centers was introduced and later rejected in Granville Township, Pennsylvania.

“A farm makes the most sense because farmers are struggling,” Zangari said. “There are a lot of people that don't want to farm anymore so they're realizing they can't pass it down to their kids. And now somebody walks in with a check for hundreds of thousands of dollars more than maybe what their farm is worth and so it's the easiest low hanging fruit.”

Increases in data center development are also not expected to stop anytime soon with an April 2025 research article published in McKinsey Quarterly predicting that data centers will require $6.7 trillion in funding globally by 2030 to keep up with demands for more computing power. AI data centers are expected to account for $5.2 trillion.

Why, and how, new data centers are being opposed

The expansion of data center development has also drawn backlash both nationally and worldwide due to the impacts these facilities have on the environment and surrounding communities.

In the United States alone, the actions of activist groups and the general public has resulted in the blockage or delay of $64 billion worth of data center projects between May 2024 and March 2025, per a report by Data Center Watch.

“Opposition to data center construction is largely motivated by local concerns,” the report said. “While the exact reasons opponents cite vary from location to location, some common themes are higher utility bills, water consumption, noise, impact on property value, and green space preservation.”

Opponents of data centers also point to the deployment and use of AI-powered surveillance systems, such as cameras made by Flock Safety and Axon, as another reason why they are fighting proposals for their construction.

These and other concerns have already fueled several movements to oppose data center development in Pennsylvania.

A Morning Call article said residents opposed to data center proposals in the region had banded together to protest them through means such as petitions, door-knocking campaigns and forming nonprofits to fundraise legal challenges.

Governments work to enact regulations

Opposition towards data centers remains a largely bipartisan issue, especially ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, both Democrats and Republicans across the United States having enacted legislation to rein in their development, ranging from regulations to moratoriums banning new proposals.

In a May 27 press release, Gov. Josh Shapiro — who is competing for reelection in the midterms against Republican candidate Stacy Garrity — released the full contents for a series of his Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development standards for data center development in the Commonwealth.

The bill, codified as HB 2650, would make GRID state law, and has already passed through the Pennsylvania House of Representatives on June 24. It has not yet been approved by the Republican-controlled Senate.

On Aug. 18 and in an effort to circumvent the gridlock between the House and Senate, Shapiro signed an executive order directing the Department of Environmental Protection to only review projects by data center developers who have made “a legally binding commitment” to have their proposals meet the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development’s standards and have received local approval.

Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania Political and Legislative Director Katie Blume, of Millheim, Pennsylvania, said she attributes the midterm elections as one of the primary reasons why many politicians, especially those in Pennsylvania, are now expressing support for data center regulations.

Blume, however, said the executive orders don’t cause these policies to become law, and that Shapiro’s Aug. 18 directive could be overturned by future governors since they’re not legally bound to abide by the order.

“We could have a totally different governor being sworn in on Jan. 2 and they could be like, 'I don't like this executive order,’” Blume said. “This is why legislation is so important, because things need to be codified.”

She said the reason Harrisburg has failed to pass many data center regulation bills into law is due to gridlock between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Greensburg resident and Voice of Westmoreland Organizer Rose Piern has been working to rally support in her community in opposition of a pair of data center proposals in Allegheny County’s Springdale and Westmoreland County’s Upper Burrell Township.

She said she disagrees with Shapiro’s initial support for data center development in Pennsylvania, which would allow developers to apply for the PA Permit Fast Track Program — a decision reversed by his Aug. 18 executive order — and endorsing on June 9, 2025 a $20 billion commitment from Amazon to build data centers throughout Pennsylvania beginning in Bucks and Luzerne counties.

However, Piern said he’s the best choice to pursue regulations following the midterms, as he’s “movable” to demands for regulation from constituents.

“He should go with what the most people want in his community,” Piern said.

What’s being done in State College, Centre County

Amid efforts to enact regulations, the State College Borough Council has not yet declared an official stance on the issue.

However, this has not stopped at least one of its members from expressing their views on seeing a potential data center be built in Centre County.

During their Aug. 17 meeting, council Member Susan Venegoni referenced a presentation made to the Centre Region Council of Government’s Land Use, Sustainability and Infrastructure committee detailing the potential impacts of local data center development.

Venegoni said she found it frightening to learn how much water would be used to cool data centers. The presentation said it could be up to one to five million gallons daily for a hyperscale facility using open-loop cooling to dissipate heat via evaporated water.

Despite State College not actively pursuing data center regulations of its own, several local governments within Centre County have already taken steps to pursue policies dictating how these facilities are built, despite the county not having any existing proposals.

These municipalities are barred by state law from enacting a complete ban of data centers within their borders due to Pennsylvania’s Municipal Planning Code, which states there must be zoning for all possible land uses, including data centers.

On Feb. 19, College Township voted unanimously to approve a memorandum that made amendments in their municipal codes to account for data centers. This was followed in May by ongoing discussions by Ferguson and Rush townships to enact similar legislation.

Some municipalities have also chosen to adopt language from other communities when drafting regulations for data centers. On Aug. 19, the Patton Township Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to approve an ordinance which takes cues from College Township’s data center regulations.

Blume said she is also working as a member of the Millheim Borough Council to enact a data center ordinance, whose contents she hopes will be adopted by surrounding municipalities. Piern said this could be copied by other municipalities — such as Millheim’s neighbors of Penn and Miles townships, two of seven municipalities in Centre County without zoning ordinances, and thus no control over how data centers are built.

She said having a network of “good” data center ordinances across Centre County, especially within communities without zoning ordinances such as Penn and Miles townships, makes clear to developers that they aren’t allowed to introduce proposals without consideration for the potential impacts.

“If those two places have very unregulated data centers that are doing whatever they want with the air in the water, it's going to directly affect people that are not in that municipality,” Piern said. “The more things that these data centers have to overcome in order for them to be in place, at least we know that they're the right businesses to be in these communities.”
